articles.title: Backup Verification in 2026: Exit Code 0 Is Not a Backup
articles.description: Backup Verification in 2026: Exit Code 0 Is Not a Backup A story made the rounds in a DevOps community recently, and it should make anyone who owns a cron job uncomfortable. An engineer checked on a backup script that had been running perfectly by every visible measure — green in the scheduler, exit code 0, night after night — and found it had been "succeeding" at backing up nothing at all for three weeks, ever since something upstream had quietly changed. No error. No page. Just three weeks of confidence with nothing underneath it. TL;DR: A backup job's exit code tells you the script ran, not that you have a backup. A backup is only trustworthy at four levels: (1) the artifact exists, (2) it is structurally intact, (3) it can be opened and read, and (4) it has actually been restored and the data verified. Most teams verify level 1 and stop. This guide walks a practical verification ladder — checksums, restic check, pg_restore --list, scheduled restore drills — plus the monitoring change that matters most: page on verification failure, not job failure. Originally published on DevOps Enginer. This is deliberately not a Kubernetes backup guide — cluster tooling like Velero and etcd snapshots is covered in the Kubernetes Backup and Disaster Recovery post. This is about the layer underneath every stack: database dumps, file archives, and object-storage backups, and how to prove they work before the day you need them. Why exit code 0 lies Exit code 0 means one narrow thing: the last command in your script did not report an error. It says nothing about what the script actually captured. Backup scripts fail silently in a handful of classic ways: Wrong or empty source paths. A directory gets moved, a mount fails to come up, or a path is renamed upstream. The archiver dutifully compresses an empty directory and exits 0. Your backup is a perfectly valid archive of nothing. Expired or rotated credentials. The dump tool fails to authenticate and writes a 0-byte file — or the wrapper script swallows the error, logs a warning nobody reads, and still exits successfully because the upload of that empty file worked fine. Silent partial captures. A database dump taken without the right flags can complete while missing schemas, extensions, or large objects. The file is large, recent, and wrong. The pattern underneath all of these: the job was monitored, but the backup was never verified. Those are different jobs, and they need different checks. The four levels of backup confidence A useful way to think about backup verification is as a ladder. Each level proves something the level below cannot: Level 1 — The artifact exists. A file or snapshot with the expected name appeared in the expected place, recently, with a plausible size. This is what most monitoring checks. It proves a process ran. Level 2 — The artifact is structurally intact. The archive is not truncated or bit-rotted. Checksums match; the backup tool's own integrity check confirms its internal structures — indexes, metadata, pack files — are consistent. This proves the bits survived storage. Level 3 — The artifact can be opened and read. The restore tool can actually parse the backup: list the table of contents of a dump, enumerate the files in an archive, read back a sample of the stored data. This proves the format is valid and the content is what you think it is — not an empty tree, not the wrong source. Level 4 — The artifact has been restored and the data verified. You restored it into a real (throwaway) environment and checked the result: the database answers queries, row counts and key tables look right, application files open. This is the only level that proves you can recover. Everything below it is inference. Notice what the ladder implies: levels 1–3 are cheap and automatable on every backup. Level 4 is more expensive, so you schedule it — sampled nightly or weekly, full restores on a rotation. What you cannot do is pretend level 1 is level 4. That gap is exactly where the three-weeks-of-nothing story lives. The verification ladder in practice Here is how to test yours, level by level. The examples use common tools — restic, PostgreSQL dumps, plain tarballs in object storage — but the pattern transfers to whatever you run. Level 1: existence, freshness, and size sanity Check that the newest artifact exists, is younger than your backup interval (plus slack), and is within a sane size band of its predecessors. A backup that suddenly shrinks by 90% is a failed backup wearing a success costume. # Fail loudly if no backup newer than 26 hours exists in the bucket aws s3 ls s3://my-backups/postgres/ --recursive \ | sort | tail -n 1 # Size sanity: compare today's artifact against the 7-day median # and alert if it deviates by more than ~50% Tools like restic make this easier because the repository keeps snapshot metadata: restic snapshots --last 1 --json # newest snapshot time, paths, tags restic stats # repository size trend Encode the rule: a missing, stale, or suddenly-tiny backup is a verification failure, even if the job that produced it exited 0. Level 2: structural integrity with checksums and tool-native checks If you produce plain archives, generate a checksum at backup time and verify it at check time: sha256sum -c postgres-2026-11-01.dump.sha256 gzip -t nightly-files.tar.gz # quick structural test for gzip streams restic has integrity checking built in: restic check restic check verifies the repository structure — all packs, indexes, and metadata present and consistent. It is fast and belongs in the nightly job. What it does not do by default is re-read your backup data — that is level 3. Level 3: prove it can be read back For archives, listing the contents is the minimum viable read test — it forces the tool to walk the whole structure: tar -tzf nightly-files.tar.gz > /dev/null # fails on truncation/corruption For PostgreSQL custom-format dumps, pg_restore --list parses the dump's table of contents without restoring anything: pg_restore --list postgres-2026-11-01.dump | head -n 50 Scan that listing for what should be there: your critical tables, extensions, and the expected object count. An empty dump has a valid header and almost nothing under it — this is the check that catches the "backed up nothing" failure mode. For restic, the read-back check is: restic check --read-data-subset=5% Understand the caveat before you rely on it: --read-data-subset=5% reads and verifies 5% of the data packs, not 5% of each file. It is sampling. A corrupt pack outside the sample will not be found tonight. Two practices make sampling honest: Rotate the subset. restic picks the subset deterministically from the percentage, so vary the percentage across runs (5%, 10%, 15%…) or accept that a fixed sample has fixed blind spots. Run a full read periodically. restic check --read-data (100%) on a monthly cadence closes the gaps the sampling leaves. Also add a content spot-check at this level: restore a handful of known files to a temp directory and diff them, or query the snapshot for a file you know changed yesterday. Existence of expected content is a much stronger signal than existence of an artifact. Level 4: restore drills — the only level that counts Restore into a throwaway environment and verify the result like a user would. For PostgreSQL: # Restore last night's dump into a scratch database createdb -T template0 restore_test pg_restore --no-owner --dbname=restore_test postgres-2026-11-01.dump # Then verify like the application would psql restore_test -c "SELECT count(*) FROM users;" psql restore_test -c "SELECT max(created_at) FROM orders;" Row counts in a plausible range and a recent max(created_at) on your busiest table prove the restore contains live, current data — not a skeleton schema and not last month's state. For file backups, restore the latest snapshot to a scratch path and verify file counts and a sample of checksums against expectations: restic restore latest --target /tmp/restore-test find /tmp/restore-test -type f | wc -l The drill is not done when the restore command exits 0. The drill is done when a check of the restored data passes. And time the drill: the duration you measure is your real recovery time, not the one in the runbook. Make verification a separate job that can fail The single most important structural change: verification must be its own job, with its own failure state, that runs after the backup job. Folded into the backup script, a verification failure disappears into the same green checkmark. Give it its own exit code and its own alert path. #!/usr/bin/env bash # verify-backups.sh — runs after the backup job, fails independently set -euo pipefail LATEST=$(restic snapshots --last 1 --json | jq -r '.[0].id') restic check # level 2 restic check --read-data-subset=5% # level 3 (sampled) restic restore "$LATEST" --target /tmp/restore-test --include /srv/app/config test -s /tmp/restore-test/srv/app/config/app.env # expected content present echo "backup_verification_success $(date +%s)" \ > /var/lib/node_exporter/textfile/backup_verification.prom The script writes a success timestamp only if every level passed — and that timestamp is what you monitor. Monitor the verification, not the job Alerting on "backup job failed" catches crashes. It does not catch the failure mode this article is about, because in that failure mode the job succeeds. Change what you page on: Page on verification failure. Any level failing — stale artifact, size anomaly, checksum mismatch, unreadable dump, failed drill — is a page-worthy event, because it means you currently do not have a proven backup. Page on missing success. Track "time since last successful verification" and alert when it exceeds your threshold (for a nightly cycle, ~30 hours). This dead-man's-switch pattern catches the silent cases: the verification job itself dying, the scheduler stopping, credentials expiring before the check even runs. Absence of failure is not presence of success — so monitor the presence of success. Track your verified restore point. The metric that matters in an incident is "how old is the newest backup that has passed level 4?" If that number quietly grows to three weeks, you want to know before the incident, not during it. If you use Prometheus, the textfile pattern above plus one alert — time() - backup_verification_success > 30 * 3600 — covers most of this. The tooling is not the hard part; deciding that verification failure pages like a production outage is. A restore-drill cadence you can actually keep Verification fails as a practice when it depends on someone remembering. Put it on a calendar: Cadence Scope Levels Nightly (automated) Every backup, right after it lands 1–3, with rotating read-data subsets Weekly (automated) Partial level-4: restore one database or one snapshot subset to a scratch environment; run content checks 4 (partial) Monthly (automated + reviewed) Full restore of one production system on rotation, timed end to end 4 (full) Quarterly Full restore drill treated like a game day: restore, verify, record duration and surprises, update the runbook 4 (full, measured) The rotation matters: every system should get a full restore at least once a quarter, rather than an annual hero-drill on the one system everybody already understands. Record each drill's duration — that number is your measured RTO, and it is almost always worse than the assumed one. Finding that out in a drill is the entire point. Cloud snapshots deserve a specific warning here: a snapshot of a disk or database is level 1 by default. Snapshots faithfully preserve corruption, they can be silently incomplete if taken mid-write without coordination, and "we have snapshots" has ended more than one incident review badly. Snapshots need the same ladder — restore one into an isolated instance, open it, query it — before they count as backups. Backup verification checklist Every backup has a separate verification job with its own pass/fail, running after the backup completes Level 1: freshness and size-band checks on every artifact, every cycle Level 2: checksums verified for plain archives; restic check (or your tool's equivalent) nightly Level 3: read-back tests — pg_restore --list, tar -t, restic check --read-data-subset with rotating percentages, plus expected-content spot checks Level 4: automated partial restores weekly; full restores monthly on rotation; quarterly timed drill Monitoring pages on verification failure and on missing verification success (~30h for nightly cycles) "Age of newest level-4-verified backup" is a visible metric, not a surprise Restore durations are recorded, so your RTO is measured rather than assumed Snapshots are restore-tested like any other backup before being trusted FAQ Is restic check on its own enough? It covers level 2 well and, with --read-data-subset, samples level 3. It never restores anything, so it cannot prove level 4. Treat it as the nightly baseline, not the whole strategy. Doesn't all this verification double my costs? Levels 1–3 are metadata, checksums, listings, and sampled reads — cheap. Level 4 restores cost scratch compute for a few hours a month. Compare that with the cost of discovering, mid-incident, that the backups were empty. My backups are managed by my cloud provider. Am I covered? Managed backup services still produce artifacts that can be empty, misconfigured, or pointed at the wrong source. The provider runs the job; verification that the artifact restores your data is still yours. What is the one change to make first? Add the dead-man's-switch alert on "time since last successful verification." It is a small change, and it converts the worst failure mode — silent, indefinite, total — into a page within a day. Summary An exit code tells you a script ran. A trustworthy backup has been checked at four levels: it exists, it is intact, it can be read, and it has been restored with the data verified. Automate the first three nightly; schedule the fourth — weekly partials, monthly full restores on rotation, quarterly timed drills. And page when verification fails or goes missing, not merely when a job crashes. The engineer in the opening story had monitoring. What they did not have was a single check that asked the only question that matters: if I needed this backup tonight, could I restore it? Build the checks that answer that question while the answer is still cheap.

articles.title: How I Built a Telegram Bot That Downloads YouTube Music & Videos (Up to 2 GB) And How yt-dlp Actually Bypasses YouTube's Protection
articles.description: Live Bot: @songsuperzxbot Source Code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot HD Demo: Watch on Streamable I built a Telegram bot that downloads music and videos from YouTube and I want to walk you through exactly how it works, including the part that most tutorials skip: how yt-dlp actually gets past YouTube's stream protection. I built a Telegram bot that downloads music and videos from YouTube — and I want to walk you through exactly how it works, including the part that most tutorials skip: how yt-dlp actually gets past YouTube's stream protection. You can try the live bot here: @songsuperzxbot on Telegram Full source code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot The Problem With Every Other Telegram Music Bot Most Telegram music bots you find online have the same three problems: They stop working after a few days because YouTube changes something They hit Telegram's 50 MB limit and either fail silently or send a compressed garbage file They run on a single thread, so if three people use it at once, everyone waits I wanted to fix all three. Here's how. How YouTube Stream Extraction Actually Works (The "Bypass" Explained) This is the part nobody explains properly. When you open a YouTube video in your browser, the actual MP4/audio stream isn't directly accessible at a clean URL. YouTube obfuscates it in two ways: 1. Signature Cipher YouTube wraps the stream URL inside a JavaScript function that scrambles the signature parameter. The raw URL looks something like this: (https://rr3---sn-xxx.googlevideo.com/videoplayback?...&sig=SCRAMBLED_SIG) The actual playable URL only works when you un-scramble that signature. YouTube's own player does this in the browser using a JavaScript function it downloads fresh every session. The function changes regularly to break scrapers. yt-dlp's solution: It downloads YouTube's player JS, extracts the current cipher function, reverse-engineers the transformation steps (they're always a combination of reverse, swap, and splice operations), and applies them to reconstruct the real signature. This is why yt-dlp updates so frequently — YouTube rotates this function. 2. n-parameter Throttling Even with a valid signature, YouTube adds an n parameter to the URL that limits download speed to about 50 KB/s if not decrypted. yt-dlp decrypts it using the same JS extraction approach, unlocking full speed. In my bot, I run yt-dlp with 8 parallel fragment streams to max out the download speed: ydl_opts = { 'concurrent_fragment_downloads': 8, 'cookiefile': 'cookies.txt', # handles age-restricted content 'quiet': True, } The cookies.txt handles age-restricted videos. You export your browser cookies with the Get cookies.txt extension and drop the file in the bot's folder. What Happens After Download: The FFmpeg Pipeline Once yt-dlp pulls the raw stream, FFmpeg takes over. For audio: # Extract audio and convert to MP3 at chosen bitrate ffmpeg -i input.webm -vn -ab 320k -ar 44100 output.mp3 For video, I use Intel VAAPI hardware acceleration when available, which runs about 10x faster than CPU encoding: # Hardware-accelerated H.264 encode ffmpeg -vaapi_device /dev/dri/renderD128 \ -i input.webm \ -vf 'format=nv12,hwupload' \ -c:v h264_vaapi \ -c:a aac output.mp4 On machines without VAAPI (Windows, Termux, most VPS), it falls back to software encoding automatically. The 50 MB Telegram Limit — How I Send Up to 2 GB Standard Telegram bots can only send files under 50 MB. Most bots just compress the video into a potato-quality file. Mine doesn't. The routing logic works like this: Under 48 MB → Send directly via standard Bot API. Instant. Over 48 MB, MTProto configured → Use native MTProto client (Telethon) which supports up to 2 GB natively with your API ID and hash from my.telegram.org Over 48 MB, no MTProto → Split the file into 44 MB chunks using lossless stream copy (zero re-encoding, zero quality loss, runs at disk speed) The lossless chunking command looks like this: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c copy -f segment \ -segment_size 46137344 chunk_%03d.mp4 No quality loss. No waiting for re-encode. Just pure stream splitting. Database: Why SQLite Was the Right Choice I went with SQLite in WAL mode instead of PostgreSQL. For a single bot, this was the right call: WAL mode means readers and writers don't block each other — critical when multiple users are downloading simultaneously Zero ops overhead — no separate database server to manage Atomic crash recovery built in Every connection opens with: The schema tracks every user, every search, every download, and aggregated stats in real time. Security: Blocking SSRF Attacks When users send URLs, a naive bot would just forward them to yt-dlp. That's dangerous — someone could send http://192.168.1.1/admin and probe your internal network. My validator rejects anything that isn't a real YouTube URL: YOUTUBE_REGEX = re.compile( r'^https?://(www\.)?(youtube\.com/watch\?v=|youtu\.be/|' r'youtube\.com/shorts/)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{11}' ) def validate_url(url): # Block private IP ranges first if re.match(r'https?://(localhost|127\.|10\.|192\.168\.|169\.254\.)', url): return False return bool(YOUTUBE_REGEX.match(url)) Filenames are also sanitized before hitting the filesystem to prevent path traversal: safe_name = re.sub(r'[^\w\-_\. ]', '_', raw_name)[:200] Running 24/7 on Android (Yes, Really) One of the coolest deployment options is Termux on Android. No root required: pkg install python ffmpeg -y python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt termux-wake-lock python bot.py The termux-wake-lock command prevents Android from killing the process when the screen turns off. I ran it for a week on an old Redmi phone and it handled hundreds of downloads without a single crash. The Test Suite: 30 Tests in 4 Seconds Everything is tested — URL validation, filename sanitization, FFmpeg processing, rate limiting, cancellation, and the database: pytest tests/ -v # 30 passed in 4.01s The cancellation test is my favourite — it verifies that hitting the Cancel button actually kills both the yt-dlp subprocess AND the FFmpeg process immediately, then confirms the temp directory is cleaned up. No zombie processes. Try It Yourself Live bot: https://t.me/songsuperzxbot on Telegram Source code + full setup guide: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot If you have questions about the yt-dlp cipher extraction, the MTProto upload integration, or running it on Termux, ask in the comments. Happy to go deeper on any part.

articles.title: How to Fix 429 Too Many Requests in Laravel: Throttle and Rate Limiting Done Right
articles.description: You push to production, traffic grows, and suddenly your logs fill with 429 Too Many Requests in Laravel. Legitimate users see "Too Many Attempts", your mobile app starts failing, and your first instinct is to just turn the throttle off. That fixes it for a day. Then the bots find the endpoint, and you are debugging a very different problem at 3 a.m. This guide walks through every real cause of the 429 Too Many Requests error in Laravel, how to diagnose which one is biting you, and working code that fixes it without leaving your app unprotected. Everything below is tested against Laravel 11 and 12, where the api throttle middleware and named rate limiters work the same way. What the 429 Error Actually Means in Laravel The 429 Too Many Requests response comes from Laravel's throttle middleware. Every request that passes through it gets counted against a named limit — for example, 60 requests per minute. When the count for a key exceeds the limit, Laravel throws a ThrottleRequestsException and responds with 429. The important part is the key. Laravel counts attempts per key, and that key is built from the limiter you configured: usually the user's ID for logged-in users, or the IP address for guests. Most 429 Too Many Requests problems in Laravel are not about traffic being too high — they are about the key or the limiter being wrong. Every 429 response also carries a Retry-After header telling the client how many seconds to wait. If your custom error handling drops that header, API clients have no way to back off gracefully, and they hammer the endpoint again the moment they retry. Cause 1 — The Default API Throttle Is Too Strict Fresh Laravel apps ship with the api limiter set to 60 requests per minute per user or IP. That is fine for a toy project. A real dashboard with auto-refresh, polling, or a chatty mobile client can burn through 60 requests in seconds. Diagnose it first. Before changing anything, confirm the throttle middleware is actually attached to the route you think it is: php artisan route:list -v | grep throttle If the 429 responses carry an X-RateLimit-Remaining header that bottoms out at exactly 60, you are hitting the default api limiter. The fix is to define your own limiter with a sane budget instead of accepting the default. In Laravel 11 and 12, you define named limiters in your application's bootstrap: use Illuminate\Http\Request; use Illuminate\Support\Facades\RateLimiter; use Illuminate\Cache\RateLimiting\Limit; RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) { return Limit::perMinute(300)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip()); }); This raises the budget to 300 per minute and, crucially, keys it on the user ID when someone is logged in. IP-keyed limits are dangerous for authenticated users: one office behind a NAT gateway shares a single IP, and five employees can exhaust a guest budget before any one of them looks abusive. Cause 2 — Two Endpoints Sharing One Limiter Inline limits like throttle:60,1 are easy to write and easy to regret. When you apply throttle:api to two different endpoints, both draw from the same budget. A webhook receiver and your search endpoint should never share a limit — one bursty integration drains the budget and the other starts 429-ing real users. The fix is one named limiter per behavior: RateLimiter::for('webhooks', fn (Request $request) => Limit::perMinute(600)->by($request->ip())); RateLimiter::for('search', fn (Request $request) => Limit::perMinute(120)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip())); Route::post('/webhooks/stripe', [WebhookController::class, 'store']) ->middleware('throttle:webhooks'); Route::get('/search', [SearchController::class, 'index']) ->middleware('throttle:search'); This is the same isolation principle behind good API design: if you are building endpoints that third parties will hit at unpredictable rates, it pays to design them as a proper custom REST API from the start (https://webixyhub.com/blog/custom-rest-api-development-cost-hiring-guide) — isolated limits, versioned routes, and documented Retry-After behavior included. Cause 3 — Behind a Proxy, Every Request Has the Same IP This is the most common 429 Too Many Requests cause in production Laravel apps and the least obvious. When your app sits behind a load balancer, Cloudflare, or a reverse proxy, every request arrives from the proxy's IP. If your limiter keys on IP, all of your traffic — every user, every bot — counts as one person. The symptom: 429s spike immediately after a deploy or a traffic surge, the X-Forwarded-For header looks fine, but the throttled IP in your logs is always your proxy. The fix is to tell Laravel which proxies to trust. In Laravel 11+, add this to your bootstrap: ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware) { $middleware->trustProxies(at: ['*']); }) In production, never use at: ['*'] blindly — list your actual proxy addresses or CIDR ranges so clients cannot spoof X-Forwarded-For. Trusting the right proxies restores the real client IP, and your per-IP limits start working the way you intended. Cause 4 — File Cache Across Multiple Servers Laravel's throttle middleware stores its counters in the cache. If CACHE_DRIVER is set to file and you run two or more app servers, each server counts independently. Your effective limit is the configured limit multiplied by the number of servers, and worse, counters are never shared, so behavior looks random: a request fails on server A and succeeds on server B. The fix: use Redis (or Memcached) as the cache driver in any environment with more than one server: CACHE_DRIVER=redis With Redis the counters are atomic, fast, and shared across all servers. This one config change turns your rate limit from an estimate into an actual guarantee. Cause 5 — The throttleApi Error on Every Request In Laravel 11+, if you enable the api throttle with a named limiter that you never defined — for example, calling $middleware->throttleApi() and then attaching throttle:api to routes without a RateLimiter::for('api') definition — every API request 429s or errors from the first call. The symptom is unmistakable: a brand-new user makes one request and gets 429. The fix is to always define the limiter you reference. If you do not need per-user nuance, the simplest correct definition is: RateLimiter::for('api', fn (Request $request) => Limit::perMinute(60)); No reference to a limiter anywhere means no mystery errors. Run php artisan route:list -v after wiring everything up and read the middleware column line by line. Cause 6 — Login and Auth Routes Keyed Wrong Auth endpoints deserve their own strict limit, keyed on more than just the email. A common setup limits logins per email, but then one attacker brute-forcing a single account burns through legitimate users' budgets, or worse, the lockout becomes a tool for denying real users access. A robust login limiter keys on the email plus the IP, and the whole flow clears the counter on success so a legitimate user starts fresh: public { $key = 'login:' . $request->ip() . '|' . strtolower($request->input('email')); RateLimiter::clear($key); $request->session()->regenerate(); return response()->json(['message' => 'Authenticated.']); } Four methods do all the work here: RateLimiter::hit records an attempt, tooManyAttempts checks the count, clear resets it after a successful login, and availableIn returns the seconds until the limit resets so you can feed a honest Retry-After to the client. Never reveal how many attempts were made or whether the account exists — a generic message plus retry timing keeps brute-force attackers from enumerating users. Apply the same discipline to password resets, registration, OTP resends, and email verification: these are the endpoints bots actually attack. Handling 429 Gracefully Instead of Swallowing It Whatever you do, keep the Retry-After header in your 429 responses. If you customize the exception rendering, pass the headers through: use Illuminate\Http\Exceptions\ThrottleRequestsException; return parent::render($request, $exception); Logging every 429 with the IP and URL gives you the evidence trail you need. When a legitimate integration starts failing, you will see the pattern in minutes instead of guessing. And on the client side, respect the header: exponential backoff on 429 and 5xx responses is the difference between a retry that works and a retry storm. Testing Your Limits Before You Ship Do not trust a limiter you have never triggered. The cheapest verification is a curl loop from two machines against your real environment — your local setup cannot reproduce proxy IPs, shared caches, or real client behavior: for i in $(seq 1 70); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{header_json} \n" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ https://webixyhub.com/api/search?q=demo done | sort | uniq -c You are looking for the first 60 responses to be 200 and the 61st onward to be 429 with a Retry-After header present. If 429s arrive early, your key is wrong (check trusted proxies). If they never arrive, your limiter is not attached or your cache driver is array in a real environment. The 429 Checklist One named limiter per behavior, never shared across unrelated endpoints. Limits keyed on user ID for authenticated traffic, IP only for guests. Trusted proxies configured with real addresses before launch, not after the first incident. Redis or another shared cache driver in production. Auth endpoints limited on email plus IP, with the counter cleared on successful login. Retry-After preserved in every custom 429 response. And a curl test against the real environment before you call it done. Rate limiting is one of those invisible engineering decisions that separates a side project from production software — like fixing the Stripe webhook signature verification flow (https://webixyhub.com/blog/fix-stripe-webhook-signature-verification-failed-laravel) or the N+1 query problem in Laravel (https://webixyhub.com/blog/fix-n1-query-problem-laravel-eager-loading), it only matters when it breaks, and then it matters a lot. Need a Developer Who Gets This Right the First Time? I am Ayesha Khan, a full-stack web developer building Laravel applications, REST APIs, and integrations for clients worldwide. If rate limiting, API design, or a tricky Laravel bug is eating your week, I can take it off your plate. Reach out through https://webixyhub.com and tell me what is breaking — or see how I evaluate Laravel expertise when teams ask me to vet one (https://webixyhub.com/blog/hire-laravel-developer-guide).

articles.title: What I learned building a Chrome extension for X growth as a student founder
articles.description: In July 2026 I started building GrowX, a Chrome extension that helps creators and founders grow a relevant audience on X (formerly Twitter). I'm a full-time student, so every decision had to fit around classes and exams. Four months later the extension is live on the Chrome Web Store, and I've learned more about product building, browser engineering and distribution than any course has taught me. Here are the lessons I'd share with any student thinking about shipping a side project. 1. Start from a workflow you already do by hand GrowX didn't start as an idea. It started as a chore. I was trying to grow my own X account, and the only thing that reliably worked was finding people who had recently followed creators in my niche, checking whether they were active and real, and engaging with them. It worked, but it took an hour a day. When a manual process works but costs too much time, that's a strong signal for a product. You already know the steps, you know what "good" looks like, and you are your own first user. Every feature in GrowX maps to a step I used to do myself: source targeting, filtering by activity and profile quality, and tracking who followed back. 2. Make the core logic explainable The heart of GrowX is a follow-back score from 1 to 99. I could have tried to build something clever and opaque. Instead I built a weighted score from a handful of signals anyone can understand: follow ratio, recent activity, whether an account has a real photo and bio, and how similar it is to accounts that followed you back before. Explainable logic paid off in three ways. Users trust a number they can reason about. Bugs are easy to find, because when a score looks wrong you can see which signal caused it. And I could ship it in days instead of weeks. For an early product, "simple and transparent" beats "smart and mysterious". 3. Local-first is a feature, not just a cost saving As a student I couldn't afford servers, so GrowX stores everything in the browser's own storage. There's no account to create and no backend holding anyone's X data. Follower snapshots, scores and settings never leave the user's machine, and backup is a JSON file they control. What started as a budget constraint turned into one of the things users mention most. People are tired of handing their social accounts to third-party dashboards. Keeping data local made the product easier to trust and easier to explain. 4. Learn your platform's constraints early Chrome's Manifest V3 replaced always-on background pages with service workers that the browser can suspend at any moment. My first scheduler kept losing its place. The fix was to treat every step as resumable: wake up with chrome.alarms, read state from storage, do one small unit of work, save state, and go back to sleep. The broader lesson is that every platform has rules that shape your architecture, whether that's a browser, an app store or a social network's own policies. Reading them on day one saves a rewrite on day thirty. It's also why GrowX defaults to slow, human-paced activity with daily caps, active hours and an emergency stop: X's rules apply to every user, and the product should respect them by design. 5. Measure what actually drives results I added analytics to GrowX mostly for myself, and it changed how I grew my own account. When I tracked which source accounts brought real follow-backs, I found that two out of ten were responsible for most of my growth. I had been spreading effort evenly across all of them. The same applies to building a product. I now track which launch channels send visitors to growxapp.org, and the answer is rarely the one I expected. 6. Distribution is half the work I underestimated this badly. Building the extension took weeks; getting anyone to see it is an ongoing job. Over the past few weeks I've listed GrowX on startup directories, written technical articles about how the follow-back score and unfollower tracker work, and shared it in communities that welcome makers. What I've learned: be honest that it's your own project, give people something useful even if they never install it, and don't expect any single launch to change everything. Search visibility compounds slowly. 7. Protect your time Exams don't move for product launches. I keep a short daily list (one piece of content, a few listings, one useful post) and automate what I can. Shipping small and steady has worked far better for me than weekend sprints followed by weeks of silence. What GrowX does today GrowX is free on the Chrome Web Store. It includes source-based audience targeting with filters, the 1-99 follow-back score, an unfollower tracker, a post scheduler with active hours, growth analytics, and an on-device writing helper. Premium options come with a 30-day free trial. Website: growxapp.org Chrome Web Store: GrowX on the Chrome Web Store If you're a student building something on the side, I'd love to hear what you're working on and what's been hardest for you. And if you try GrowX, honest feedback is the most useful thing you can give me.

articles.title: Aging NASA Telescope Expected to Crash Back to Earth in Days
articles.description: Aging NASA telescope the Swift Observatory is expected to fall back to Earth by Friday after a failed attempt to rescue it last week. Most of the one-and-a-half-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere as it falls, but some pieces made of dense tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, Brad Cenko, the mission’s chief scientist, told the Associated Press. Any surviving wreckage will most likely end up in the ocean. But parts of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The Swift Observatory is a 22-year-old telescope launched into orbit on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for gamma-ray bursts and supernovas. Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual, but the telescope was never expected to stay in space for good. “We’ve known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic,” Pennsylvania State University’s John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team, said. Swift captured more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, 1,400 exploding stars, a slew of comets, asteroids, and star-shredding black holes. The telescope was able to swiftly swivel—the source of its name—toward erupting celestial events. Read it at Associated Press Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: Could AI give older creatives a second act?
articles.description: Advertising is made for the young by the young. That’s conventional wisdom backed up by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which in 2025 reported the median age of ad industry workers was 39, compared to 42 for the broader workforce. Meanwhile, a report from the World Advertising Research Center estimates that only 5% to 10% of budgets are directed toward older consumers. Today, brands focus on Gen Z customers and ad companies target Gen Z hires, all on newer platforms like TikTok. As the new guard sweeps in, the people who built the previous era creep toward irrelevance. As AI is impacting every aspect of the industry, it’s only natural to assume that it, too, will usher in a new era of ad makers and consumers. It doesn’t have to. Some of the most compelling artists who incorporate AI I encounter are not necessarily very young workers coming straight out of school. They are older, established game designers, VFX artists, concept artists, animators, photographers, and directors who have spent decades devising concepts and developing characters, images, and entire imaginary worlds that have earned fandoms. These professionals have played with light, composition, performance, movement, texture, and narrative. They know how to make the moment big and cinematic and, more importantly, they pick up on when it feels wrong. AI can generate campaigns, but it cannot replicate genuine experience. And if these experienced workers can leverage the technology, it could, potentially, revitalize their careers. The Last Generation of Analog Talent The common assumption is that AI belongs to digital natives. But knowing how to run a new model is not the same as knowing what to create with it. Those who came up in the analog era can immediately discern when an image lacks tension or a lens choice feels off. They know when a character could go viral and move them to the front of the scene. That’s judgment that comes with experience, not with AI. Great things happen when proven talents are unleashed in new areas: Think of editors generating the images they once had to search for, or a game designer taking their vision to directing a commercial shoot. It’s understandable, though, that agencies recruit youth for AI. After all, the algorithm on career sites seeks AI talent based on specific tool fluency, and doesn’t delve into broader AI exposure and career experience. But those who are looking find a technologically attuned older workforce. A new report by job training nonprofit CWI Works and IPSOS found that 90% of people 55 and older who have used AI for work were somewhat comfortable with AI, and 50% were extremely comfortable using it. Among Gen X respondents, 71% have used generative AI, tracking right alongside the 74% of millennials. This is not a closed-minded cohort. Just because someone isn’t a 22-year-old grad doesn’t mean they’re not curious about this tool. That curiosity, combined with decades of experience, is a powerful thing. Prompting is not the profession AI skills matter, but new tools expire quickly. Today’s specialization is tomorrow’s button click. Taste, however, can never become a button. I have worked as a copywriter and creative director at agencies for a decade. When I started Dolsten & Co. 18 months ago as an AI-first creative agency and production company, I was building something new but was inspired by the stellar talent I’d learned from through my career. In recent months, Dolsten & Co. brought in an experienced copywriter, game designer, and storyboard artist with decades of experience to work on board. The copywriter built an immersive digital experience for us, while we enlisted the game designer to build a world for a TV commercial, and the storyboard artist shaped a beautiful narrative for a brand film. Their careers had been displaced by industry upheaval and hiring biases—consolidations, cost cutting, and a push for offices to “look” younger—but talent remains, and the three are shaping brand narratives and AI-driven content for leading brands using their rich experience. I knew that the AI skills would come, and that they’d enable these kinds of valuable, second-act experts to bring incredible ideas to life. Our hiring philosophy has brought incredibly diverse talent. Experience is never obsolete Advertising is notoriously dismissive of older creative talent. Experience is expensive, and senior people are pushed toward smaller management pools. Specialists can find their craft devalued when the industry adopts a different production model. These are valid reasons for the talent drain, but AI creates the possibility of a different trajectory. This doesn’t mean younger creators are less important. The most interesting teams combine youth’s speed, experimentation, and cultural fluency with the judgment and discipline of experienced artists. AI will continue to automate certain tasks and compress workflows. As the creative industry dwells on what AI is replacing, the more provocative question is who it will allow to begin again.

articles.title: How does one nudge ripple through ten layers?
articles.description: The chain rule, the idea that lets a network see through every one of its layers, with real numbers. A neural network is a chain. The input goes into the first layer, the first layer's output goes into the second, and so on, until the last layer produces an answer and a loss, one number that says how wrong that answer is. Training keeps asking one question: if I nudge this weight a little, how much does the loss move? For a weight ten layers down, the nudge has to travel through every layer above it before it reaches the loss. The chain rule tells you how big it is when it arrives. A network is a chain Written as math, a ten-layer network is a function inside a function inside a function: f₁₀( ⋯ f₂( f₁(x) ) ⋯ ) Picture it as a tower of dials on one shaft: the input at the bottom, a dial for each layer above it. Turn the bottom dial a little and every dial above it turns too, but not by the same amount. Each layer has its own ratio, which can make the turn bigger or smaller. A network as a tower of dials. Turn the input at the bottom and every layer above it turns; the blue wedges show how far each one moved. Two links, real numbers Take just two layers. The first triples its input, y = 3x, and the second squares that, z = y². Start the input at x = 1: then y = 3 and z = 9. Now raise the input by 0.01, to x = 1.01. Then y = 3.03: it moved 0.03, three times the nudge, so its ratio is 3. And z = 3.03² = 9.1809: it moved about 0.18, six times y's own move of 0.03, so its ratio is 6. Why six? Write out (3 + h)² = 9 + 6h + h². For a tiny h, the h² hardly matters, so the change is about 6h. That ratio is the slope of y² at y = 3: its derivative. Close on two links. Raising the input by 0.01 moves the first layer by 0.03 (ratio 3) and the second by 0.18 (ratio 6). The ratios multiply The first link multiplies the nudge by 3 and the second by 6, so together it's 3 × 6 = 18. The real numbers agree: z moved 0.18 for a nudge of 0.01, which is 18 times. That's the chain rule. Written with derivatives: dz/dx = dz/dy · dy/dx = 6 × 3 = 18 Each layer only needs to know its own slope: find each link's ratio where it stands, then multiply. You've seen this on a clock A clock is a chain too. The minute hand turns 12 times as fast as the hour hand, and the second hand turns 60 times as fast as the minute hand. So the second hand turns 12 × 60 = 720 times as fast as the hour hand: you multiply the ratios along the chain, exactly as with the layers. Ten layers, ten ratios A network with ten layers multiplies ten ratios, and a product of many numbers moves fast in both directions. If every layer halves the turn, the top moves 0.5¹⁰ ≈ 0.001 as far as the input. The nudge has all but vanished. If every layer doubles it, the top moves 2¹⁰ = 1024 times as far. The nudge has exploded. Ten layers that each double the turn. The bottom barely moves, and the top spins 1024 times as far. This is why very deep networks were once so hard to train: the signal about how a deep weight affects the loss either faded away or grew out of control. The same rule in a real network Here is a small three-layer network: two inputs, three hidden neurons with ReLU, and one output, scored by squared error against a target of 1. With inputs 2 and 1, the hidden neurons come out at 1, 0.5 and 0.2, the output is 3, and the loss is (3 − 1)² = 4. Pick one weight, w = 0.5, from the first input to the top hidden neuron, and follow its path to the loss. It has three links: the hidden neuron moves 2 times as much as w (the input it multiplies is 2); the output moves 3 times as much as that hidden neuron (its weight is 3); the loss moves 4 times as much as the output (the slope of (y − 1)² at y = 3). So ∂L/∂w = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24. Check it: raise w from 0.50 to 0.51, and the loss goes from 4.00 to 4.24. A three-layer network. One weight's path to the loss has ratios 2, 3 and 4, so the loss moves 24 times as much as the weight. Try it in PyTorch PyTorch applies the chain rule for you. torch.func.grad returns a function's derivative, even when the function is a chain of other functions: from torch import tensor, func y = lambda x: 3 * x z = lambda y: y ** 2 f = lambda x: z(y(x)) x = tensor(1.) print(func.grad(f)(x)) It prints tensor(18.), the same 3 × 6 we found by hand. Add a third layer that halves its input, and the gradient of the longer chain should come out at 9. Key takeaways A network is a chain of layers, and a nudge at the bottom ripples through every layer above it. Each layer scales the nudge by its own ratio: its local slope, the derivative. The chain rule: multiply the ratios along the chain. dz/dx = dz/dy · dy/dx. With many layers the product can shrink to almost nothing (0.5¹⁰ ≈ 0.001) or blow up (2¹⁰ = 1024). In a real network, a weight's effect on the loss is the product of the ratios along its path: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24. This article is part of Deep Learning, Visually by Logit Solutions AI: short animated explainers that cover one idea at a time, each with a written version like this one.

articles.title: WARN Act and Health Insurance: What Happens to Your Coverage After a Layoff
articles.description: WARN Act and Health Insurance: What Happens to Your Coverage After a Layoff A WARN notice tells you when your job is scheduled to end. It does not, by itself, tell you when your health insurance ends — and that gap catches many workers by surprise. The WARN Act is a notice law, not a benefits law. It requires qualifying employers to give 60 days' advance notice of a mass layoff or plant closing, but it does not set the date your health coverage stops, and it does not pay your premiums. That makes health coverage a separate question to answer as soon as a notice arrives. The figures below set the scale: as of November 1, 2026, Layoff Atlas tracks 686 WARN notices covering 66,703 reported workers in its 90-day notice window, with 29 counts unavailable. California (17,715 workers) and Washington (17,361) lead the state ranking, followed by Illinois (4,385), Texas (3,280), and Georgia (2,492). These are reported plans, not confirmed job losses — but every filing behind them represents workers who will face the same coverage question. First, find your actual end date Do not assume coverage ends on your last day of work. Many employer plans run through the end of the month in which employment ends; some stop on the termination date itself. The answer is in your plan documents or your benefits letter, and it is worth confirming in writing before your last day. Also check whether your notice period changes anything: if you keep working through a 60-day notice period, you generally keep the coverage that comes with that employment. COBRA: the bridge most workers hear about first If your employer has 20 or more employees and offers a group health plan, federal COBRA usually lets you keep that same plan for up to 18 months after a layoff, by paying the full premium yourself plus a small administrative fee. You typically have 60 days from the later of your coverage loss date or the date you receive the COBRA election notice to choose it, and coverage can be retroactive to the loss date if you elect and pay within that window. That retroactivity matters: it means you do not have to decide on day one. You can check whether another option is cheaper, and still elect COBRA within the window if you need care in the meantime — but only if you pay the premiums back to the loss date. Miss the deadline, and the option closes. Smaller employers are not covered by federal COBRA, but many states run "mini-COBRA" continuation laws for groups of fewer than 20 employees, often for shorter periods. Your state's insurance department or your former employer's benefits administrator can confirm which rule applies to you. The ACA marketplace: a second, often cheaper, door Losing job-based coverage also triggers a special enrollment period on the Affordable Care Act marketplace, generally 60 days from the loss of coverage. Unlike COBRA, marketplace coverage is priced on your income, and subsidies can make it far cheaper than paying a full group premium — especially if your household income drops after the layoff. Marketplace plans also start prospectively, not retroactively, so timing matters: apply promptly rather than waiting until the end of the window. Compare the two on total cost, not just the monthly premium. A marketplace plan may have a lower premium but a higher deductible, and switching plans resets your progress toward that year's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. If you have already met a large deductible under your employer plan, staying on COBRA for the rest of the plan year can sometimes be cheaper overall, even with a higher premium. What about dependents, prescriptions, and ongoing care? Coverage questions are family questions. COBRA and marketplace enrollment each let you cover eligible dependents, but a spouse with their own employer plan may have a separate special enrollment window — usually 30 days under an employer plan, shorter than the marketplace's 60. If your spouse can join their employer's plan, that deadline is the one to watch first. For ongoing treatment, check whether your doctors are in-network under any new plan before you switch, and ask your pharmacy about a bridge supply of regular prescriptions. A mid-year plan change can also mean new prior-authorization requirements, so request those early rather than discovering them at the pharmacy counter. A checklist for the notice period Confirm your coverage end date in writing, and whether it runs to month-end. Note your COBRA election deadline and your marketplace special enrollment deadline — they are different clocks. Price COBRA against a marketplace plan, including deductibles already met. Check a spouse's employer-plan enrollment window, which may be only 30 days. Keep copies of every benefits letter, election notice, and payment receipt. The heaviest upcoming layoff weeks in the current data underline why this matters now: the week of November 14 alone carries 8,453 reported workers, followed by 6,925 in the week of November 21, out of 30,881 workers across the next six weeks. The workers who answer the coverage question during the notice period — rather than after coverage lapses — keep the most options open. This article is general information, not legal or benefits advice; plan rules vary by employer and state, so confirm your own dates with your plan administrator. Data source: Layoff Atlas

articles.title: Turns out I'm the one making the ghosts
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Ghost in the Machine On 8 August I committed a file called seed.sql. On 25 October I filled it in. For 78 days it was zero bytes. Nothing ever told me. The file existed. The import ran. The app worked. Only the data was missing — and an empty file doesn't raise an error. It just sits there being nothing, very quietly, for two and a half months. I found out while deploying, a few days ago. So I built something to go looking for whatever else was in there. What I Built Ghosts in the Machine reads a public repository's git history and finds failures that never produced an error — the ones nobody noticed, because there was nothing to notice. Point it at a repo. It walks the commits, finds what broke silently, and an open-weight model groups it, ranks it, and writes up what happened. a public repo │ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ │ walk history │ every commit, every diff └────────┬────────┘ │ rules │ no AI. zero-byte blobs, │ (deterministic)│ credential-shaped lines │ oddness │ no AI. size collapses, resurrected │ (deterministic)│ paths, diffs that don't match └────────┬────────┘ their own message ▼ findings, with commit hashes │ Gemma │ did this break? which of these │ (open weights) │ matter? how do I explain it? ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ what the model made of it │ ├─────────────────────────────────────┤ │ what git actually recorded │ ← both shown, so you can └─────────────────────────────────────┘ check one against the other When I ran it on my own repositories: seed.sql — committed empty, filled 78 days later requirements.txt — committed empty in the initial commit, filled 79 days later readme.md — committed empty, by a commit whose message was "Add README" A database password in three places in one commit, one of them commented out A manifest.json, empty, which I later deleted without ever noticing it held nothing Every one of those is mine. None of them ever failed. How I read the theme The organisers suggested a haunted terminal and an offline oral history tool. I went elsewhere. I kept coming back to what a ghost actually is: something present, that nobody can see, that everyone has stopped looking for. That describes a file committed empty exactly. It's in the tree. It's in every clone. It's in the history permanently. And because it never errors, nobody is looking. The repository is the haunted house. The commits are the record of who lived there. I just read the record. Who this is for The case I kept thinking about isn't mine. It's inheriting a repo. You join a team, or pick up something abandoned, and you want to know: what's wrong with this that nobody is going to tell me? The README is aspirational. The code is current. The history holds the real answers, and nobody reads 500 commits to find them. Nobody hands over a project with a list of everything quietly broken in it. Partly because it would be awkward. Mostly because they don't know either. That's the whole point — these failures produced no error, so the person who made them is as unaware as the person inheriting them. The same goes for open-sourcing something, or handing a repo to a client. What's in the history that shouldn't be? Secrets survive deletion, and people usually find that out afterwards. Demo → ghosts-in-the-machine.onrender.com Two exhibits load on arrival, from my own repositories. Paste in any public repo and it will read that one instead. It's a free instance, so the first request after a quiet spell takes a moment to wake up. Small and medium repos come back in under a minute. Large ones take longer, because cloning dominates. Code → github.com/VidhiDixit2000/ghosts-in-the-machine How I Used Open-Source AI Two layers, deliberately separated. The deterministic layer walks the history and emits findings. No AI. It checks whether a blob is zero bytes when the file extension implies content, and whether added lines look like credentials. Facts, with commit hashes attached. The model layer answers a different question: which of these matter, which are the same story, and how do I explain them to a person? That's Gemma, via OpenRouter — open weights, hosted inference, so the demo runs without a GPU. The split isn't tidiness. Each layer does what the other is bad at. A regular expression can't tell you an empty file mattered. It has no idea whether 78 days is a long time. Ask a model to scan a whole history instead and it invents findings, misses real ones, and burns tokens doing it. Here's the split earning its keep. One repo produced three separate findings: a connection string in database.py, a DATABASE_URL in docker-compose.yml, and a POSTGRES_PASSWORD in the same file. Three true findings. One story — the same password, three places, one commit. The rules found them. Only the model saw they were one ghost. On the page, both are shown. What the model made of it sits above what git actually recorded, so you read the narration and then check it against the hashes underneath. That mattered more than I expected. The model was confidently wrong, and I could prove it While I was tuning the narration prompt, Gemma 3 12B wrote this about the credentials: These values... were removed from the working tree before the commit. However, they remain present in the repository's history. That's impossible. Git history contains what was committed. If something was removed before a commit, that commit never recorded it — it wouldn't be in the history at all. The sentence contradicts itself. This was google/gemma-3-12b-it at temperature 0.3. What actually happened: committed 30 July, removed 25 October. Nearly three months apart. The findings said so correctly. The model garbled them on the way to prose. I only noticed because the evidence was sitting right underneath. If the narration had replaced the findings instead of sitting beside them, I'd have shipped a well-written falsehood about my own repository. Moving to Gemma 3 27B and lowering the temperature fixed that particular error. But the architecture caught it, not the model choice. If you're building on a model: test across versions and temperatures. A wrong answer at 0.3 looks completely reasonable until you check it against something that can't be wrong. The mistake I made, and what I did about it I started by writing rules for failures I'd personally hit. Empty files, because of seed.sql. Leaked credentials, because of a .dockerignore I forgot and a password I thought I'd deleted by commenting it out. Then I saw what I'd built: a tool that finds failures someone has already met. For a project about failures nobody noticed, that's close to self-defeating. A rule per failure type, forever, and only ever the ones already on the list. The way out isn't more rules. There are infinitely many. It's changing what the rules are for. Git's vocabulary is tiny. A file appeared, vanished, changed, or moved. Its bytes grew or shrank. That's nearly all of it. So however many ways software can break, a failure has to express itself in that vocabulary to be visible at all — and it lands in one of a few shapes: something got smaller when it shouldn't have something vanished and came back two paths that should have been one a diff that doesn't match what its message claims a change that undid an earlier change Truncated JSON and a gutted requirements.txt are different failures with the same shape. A case-only rename and a resurrected file are different failures with the same shape. So I added a second deterministic layer that names nothing. Six measurements: size collapse, a file too small for its extension, a resurrected path, two paths differing only in case, a large diff under a short message, a change that's almost all deletion. Each scores how unusual a commit is. The dozen oddest go to the model in one call, and the model says what — if anything — went wrong. Like a metal detector. It doesn't know what a coin is. It knows there's metal here. Someone else digs. The signal set is bounded by what git can record. What the model can name isn't. Here it is working. On a test repo, the oddness layer flagged a .json file deleted inside a 14,000-line commit. Neither rule would ever have caught that — it isn't empty and it isn't a credential. It surfaced because it was strange. And then the model explained it as an attempt to hide evidence. Both halves of that sentence are the point. To be honest about what this is: those six measurements are still rules. I wrote them by hand and picked every number in them. What changed is the ratio. One rule in the first layer finds one failure type, forever. One measurement in the second finds a truncated JSON, a gutted manifest, a half-written migration, a botched merge — failures I've never thought of and don't need to. The rules didn't disappear. They stopped growing with the problem. Why Open Innovation Matters This tool reads your repository. Every commit, every diff, every line that ever held a credential. If it's going to do that, you should be able to read it back: what it looks for, what it sends to a model, what it redacts before sending. The code is public for the same reason the evidence sits beside the narration. A tool making claims about your history should be checkable. Open weights meant I could reason about failure. When Gemma produced that impossible sentence, I could see which model, which version, what temperature, what prompt. I changed two of them and watched the failure go away. That's a debugging loop. Behind an opaque API it would have been a shrug. What It Doesn't Do Two named rules, six measurements. Most well-maintained repositories come back empty, correctly. The page says so rather than pretending otherwise. It doesn't read a whole repository. Commit depth is capped, and the page tells you when a history was truncated. Large repos are slow. Cloning dominates, not scanning. The model reads intent into odd commits. On a repo called buggy-python, with a commit message reading "write buggy code", it described a deleted JSON file as an attempt to hide evidence. The measurement was right that something unusual had happened. Everything after that was the model writing a story. The narration isn't stable. Same repo, same prompt, same temperature: one run called a deletion "possibly intentional experimentation", the next called it "a deliberate attempt to hide evidence". No code changed in between. It invents chronology inside a single commit. A commit is a snapshot — the changes in it have no order. I told the model that in plain words. It repeated it back correctly ("both changes were recorded in the same commit") and then wrote, one sentence later, that one happened immediately after the other. It isn't ignoring the rule. It states the rule and breaks it in the same paragraph. Secret detection is shallow next to dedicated tools. The quiet-failure half is where the gap is. Every one of those is visible on the page, because the evidence sits under the narration. That isn't a coincidence. It's why the page is built that way. What I'd Build Next Some named rules will always be worth keeping. A dependency manifest losing most of its contents is worth catching directly rather than inferring. But they shouldn't live in one growing file of conditionals. The shape that scales is a small registry. Every rule implements the same interface — does this apply to this change, and if so what does it find — and every rule returns findings in one format. Adding a rule then costs nothing structurally. Rules that don't apply to a file never run against it. Each commit is parsed once and shared. Duplicate findings collapse by fingerprint. One rule failing doesn't take the scan down. A registry to make named rules cheap, and oddness scoring to make most of them unnecessary. The first bounds the maintenance cost. The second bounds how many you need at all. The Spirit of It I'm the kind of person who commits functionality in pieces. Somewhere in all that pushing, something ends up in a file that shouldn't be there. There are mistakes in every repo I've shipped that I'd only see if I stepped away, came back, looked properly, and went wait, what? So I built something to look. It spent most of its time looking at mine. The one that got me wasn't the empty files. It was the password. I'd found it weeks earlier — a connection string in database.py — and I commented it out, felt responsible, moved on. My own tool later showed me that same line, in a commit from July, with the # still on the front. The comment character meant nothing. Git had kept it the whole time, and so had every clone anyone had ever made. Then the same password twice more, in a file I hadn't thought about. Three copies of one mistake, and I'd only ever found one. Somewhere in there it stopped feeling like I was finding ghosts and started feeling like I'd been making them. The 78-day empty file is the one I tell people about, but it isn't really a mistake. Nobody did anything wrong. A file was committed before it had content, and there was no moment at which anything would have said so. It sat there, in every clone, for two and a half months, being nothing. That's what I find unsettling about git. Your repository remembers everything you did and tells you none of it unless you go and ask. Every project I've shipped has things in it I don't know about yet. Which means the next person to open one of my repos wouldn't know either. That part I hadn't thought about until I was looking at the output. Building a ghost detector and finding five of your own is a strange way to spend a couple of days. I commit differently now. Built With Gemma (open weights) via OpenRouter — judging, grouping, narration Python, FastAPI, GitPython — detection and a single-service web app Render — hosting ElevenLabs — the voice reading you in, and the room tone underneath .tech — the domain GitHub Actions — the tool scans its own repository on every push Building a ghost detector and finding five of your own is a strange way to spend a couple of days. I commit differently now.
